To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the EBV-encoded EBNA1 protein inhibits MHC class I presentation of peptides derived from mRNAs that are translationally suppressed by the Gly-Ala repeat within EBNA1, and that the rate of translation is a key parameter for the presentation of MHC class I antigens.

EBV-EBNA1 suppresses MHC class I presentation by inhibiting translation initiation of the mRNA that is used for antigen presentation, and that the rate of translation of this mRNA is a major determinant of the level of antigen presentation.
the EBV-encoded EBNA1 Gly-Ala repeat inhibits antigen presentation via the mRNA translation initiation machinery, and that this inhibition is directly related to the translation rate of the mRNA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how viruses manipulate the immune system and the mechanisms that control antigen presentation.
the molecular mechanisms by which viruses interfere with MHC class I mediated antigen presentation.
the role of the EBV encoded EBNA1 protein in the control of antigen presentation by the major histocompatibilty (MHC) complex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the EBNA1 Gly-Ala repeat is sufficient and necessary, and that it works in cis, to prevent presentation of the antigenic peptides from the mRNA to which it is linked, by inhibiting mRNA translation initiation.
the GAr of EBNA1 suppresses translation initiation in cis and that this is sufficient and necessary for the GAr to inhibit MHC Class I presentation of peptides from the mRNA to which it is bound.
the immune system is not able to detect EBNA1 protein because the immune system does not detect the EBNA1 mRNA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EBV-encoded EBNA1 Gly-Ala repeat inhibits MHC class I mediated immune recognition of EBV infected cells by interfering with the translation initiation of mRNAs that carry the repeat.
the EBNA1 GAr inhibits antigen presentation by interfering with mRNA translation initiation.
EBV has evolved a strategy to control the MHC class I pathway via the EBNA1 GAr by suppressing translation initiation from the mRNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rate of translation of a given mRNA is an important parameter in the regulation of the MHC class I presentation pathway.
the rate of translation of a given mRNA is a key factor in determining whether it will serve as a source of antigenic peptides.
a virus can control MHC class presentation by interfering with the translation initiation of a specific mRNA.
